archetype.name: Fringe Contender (shootout offense)
archetype.definition: Detroit has an offense good enough to beat anyone and a defense bad enough to lose to anyone, which leaves a 3-2 team with middle-of-the-pack net efficiency, last in a strong division, whose ceiling rests on whether the defense can climb out of the league's basement.

report.headline: An elite offense dragging a last-ranked defense through weekly shootouts
report.take:
This is a familiar Lions shape pushed to an extreme. Jared Goff has started every game behind the league's top scoring offense (32.8 points a game) and the third-best offense by EPA, with the passing game third in EPA per play and second in success rate. The ground game adds steady efficiency, not big chunks: Jahmyr Gibbs has carried 105 times, the line ranks fourth in yards before contact and fourth in run success, and the Arizona game (163 rushing yards, 4.8 rush EPA) showed what it looks like when it all lines up. Special teams sit second in EPA per game. The problem is the other side. The defense ranks 32nd in EPA allowed, 29th in points allowed, 30th on third down and 31st in red-zone touchdown rate.

What makes the defense strange is that it does several of the hard things well. It leads the league with 20 sacks, ranks seventh in pressure rate and first in missed-tackle rate, and still gets carved up. Sacks look like boom-or-bust events here. When the rush doesn't get home, passes beat this secondary deep (29th in deep-pass EPA allowed) and short (28th). Opponents have noticed and pass against Detroit more than against any other defense. WR1s, WR2s and tight ends have all had big days. Brian Branch has not played a snap this year, and that absence is a believable part of the story.

The record is close to honest. Wins over expected sit at -0.15, the point differential implies 3.1 wins against three actual, and a 2-1 mark in one-score games isn't propping anything up. The turnover margin is the thing to distrust: the offense has given the ball away once in five games. That pace won't hold, while the defense's five takeaways (27th) is low enough that it should drift up. The market has also overrated this team. Detroit has covered only a quarter of its games while every one of them has cleared the total, which says the Book keeps pricing a better defense than the one on the field.

History says both halves are real. The 2024 team paired a top-three offense with a top-ten defense and won 15. The 2025 team kept the offense near the top but slipped to 15th on defense and finished 9-8. This year's offense looks like the 2024 version and the defense looks like the 2020 one. The rest of the season depends on how much of that gap Branch's return and a bye week can close.

strengths.title: A passing game that never stalls
strengths.body: Goff's offense is third in pass EPA and second in overall success rate. It has scored at least 26 in every game, against defenses ranked anywhere from 11th to 30th by EPA. That consistency against varied opposition, plus the 2024 track record, makes this the most bankable part of the team. The only threats to it are injury and the interior line losing Ben Bartch.

strengths.title: Efficient, well-blocked run game
strengths.body: The line gets Gibbs to contact clean, ranking fourth in yards before contact and fourth in run success. That keeps Detroit on schedule even though rush EPA (-0.033) is only good, not explosive. The weak spots are a 24th-ranked stuff rate and 30th in short-yardage conversion. The line can open lanes but struggles to move a stacked box.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Twenty sacks lead the league, and the sack rate (fourth) and QB-hit rate (sixth) back it up. This isn't one fluky game: Detroit has had five-sack games against New Orleans, the Jets and Arizona. The pressure is real. The open question is whether the coverage behind it can turn that pressure into stops.

concerns.title: Coverage is a sieve, deep and short
concerns.body: Detroit is 28th in pass EPA allowed, 29th in deep-pass EPA allowed and 26th in explosive pass rate allowed. Offenses pass on it more than on any other defense. Opposing WR1s and tight ends have scored far above their norms, so this is a structural flaw, not one bad matchup. Branch's return could help, but he hasn't played, so treat any fix as a hope, not a projection.

concerns.title: No stops when it matters
concerns.body: Opponents convert half their third downs (30th) and score touchdowns on 81% of red-zone trips (31st). That is why yardage problems turn straight into points. Some of this should regress toward average, since red-zone rates are noisy over five games. But a defense that also forces few turnovers has few ways to bail itself out.

concerns.title: Ball security will come back down
concerns.body: One offensive turnover in five games is carrying a top-ten turnover margin. No offense keeps that up, so the margin will likely shrink even if Goff plays just as well. When it does, a defense this leaky has less room for the short fields that follow.

trend.note: The offense has been a metronome, scoring 31, 31, 31, 26 and then 45 at Arizona with its best rushing day. The defense has given up 21 or more every week, and the 41 at Buffalo and 32 at Carolina were the low points, so the shape of the team hasn't changed.

nextGame.headline: Off the bye, Detroit gets a Packers front missing bodies
nextGame.body:
Detroit comes off a bye (14 days' rest) and hosts Green Bay indoors as a 3-point favorite, with a 53.5 total. Green Bay is the mirror image: a mid-pack offense (15th in EPA) built around passing, because its run game is last in EPA, yards per carry and yards before contact. Its defense is 11th by EPA and first in explosive pass rate allowed, but 27th against the run and 27th in red-zone touchdown rate. The Packers' 4-2 record leans on a perfect mark in one-score games and a league-best 11 takeaways. Their point differential is close to even.

Availability tilts toward Detroit up front. Micah Parsons is out with an ACL, and Green Bay's interior line is thin, with Javon Hargrave and Jonathan Ford on injured reserve and Jordon Riley still out. Corner Benjamin St-Juste is out and Brandon Cisse (88% of snaps) is questionable with a stinger. On Detroit's side, guard Ben Bartch (93% of snaps) is on IR. Center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch carry return estimates for this date. Corner Rock Ya-Sin is questionable with a hamstring, and linebacker Devin White is on IR.

waysToWin.title: Run Gibbs at a depleted interior
waysToWin.body: Green Bay is 27th in rush EPA allowed and ranks last in EPA allowed to opposing lead backs. That was before it lost several defensive tackles. Detroit's line is fourth in yards before contact, so this is the cleanest edge on the board. It also shortens the game and protects a bad defense.

waysToWin.title: Finish drives in the red zone
waysToWin.body: The Packers allow touchdowns on 75% of red-zone trips (27th) and are 25th on third down. Their defense makes you earn yards but folds near the goal line. Detroit's success-rate offense is built to grind out exactly those drives.

waysToWin.title: Make Love win it from behind
waysToWin.body: Green Bay can't run (last in rush EPA), so a Detroit lead turns the Packers into a pure dropback team. That plays into Detroit's league-leading sack total. Green Bay's line already ranks 29th in QB-hit rate allowed.

waysToLose.title: Packer receivers beat a leaky secondary
waysToLose.body: Detroit is a heavy pass funnel and has been torched by WR1s and WR2s. Green Bay throws to wideouts more than most teams. If Jordan Love has time, the 13th-ranked Packer passing game can look much better than its season numbers.

waysToLose.title: Turnovers finally find Detroit
waysToLose.body: Green Bay leads the league in takeaways, and Detroit's one giveaway all year is the stat most likely to snap. A couple of short fields against this defense would erase Detroit's edge on offense quickly.

waysToLose.title: No big plays over the top
waysToLose.body: Green Bay allows the fewest explosive passes in the league and ranks eighth in deep EPA allowed. If it takes away the chunk throws and Detroit's run game stalls in short yardage (30th), the Lions could be forced to settle for field goals.

nextGame.watch: Whether Branch plays and how the Detroit secondary holds up against Green Bay's wideouts. Detroit's offense should score, so the game turns on whether the defense can get one or two stops.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should keep scoring near the top of the league. Its efficiency is broad-based, it has history behind it, and it has held up against good and bad defenses. Expect a little less scoring as turnovers creep in. The 45-point Arizona game is the top of the range, not the baseline, and two meetings with Minnesota's top-ranked defense will test it. The defense is the swing. Some regression toward average is likely on red-zone and third-down rates, and Branch returning would help the coverage. Still, a unit last in EPA allowed rarely becomes good mid-season, so league-average would be a win.

The schedule is mixed. Miami, Tennessee and Tampa Bay bring bottom-three offenses, and seven of the remaining games are at home. But the closing stretch has five division games, including two against unbeaten Minnesota and road trips to Chicago and Green Bay. From fourth place in a division with no soft team, Detroit's realistic path is a wild card earned by outscoring people.
swingFactors: Branch's return and whether the secondary stabilizes
Offensive turnovers normalizing from near zero
Interior line health with Bartch on IR

confidence.note: Five games is a small sample, but the offense matches its recent history. The defensive collapse is the less certain half.
